entries.previousTitle: Dunning–Kruger Effect – when the less you know, the more confident you are
entries.title: Dunning–Kruger Effect – when performance and self-assessment do not line up
entries.description:
The Dunning–Kruger Effect describes a pattern found in some self-assessment tasks: lower performers can overestimate their performance more than higher performers do. It is about calibration between measured performance and self-assessment, not a rule that the least skilled person is always the most confident.

Where can it show up?
- Learning: a student predicts a much stronger result than an objective test later shows.
- Work skills: someone rates their performance higher than external measures or repeated results support.
- Training: confidence changes more slowly than actual performance after feedback or practice.

A better check
- Make a prediction before seeing the score or feedback.
- Compare confidence with an objective test, outcome or independent review.
- Track calibration across several attempts instead of judging from one good or bad result.
- Notice whether feedback changes both skill and self-assessment over time.
- Do not use Dunning–Kruger as a label for people you think are wrong. Experts are not automatically underconfident, and confidence alone does not diagnose the effect.
entries.reason: The legacy page repeated the popular claim that less knowledge means more confidence and that true experts underestimate themselves. The reviewed literature supports a narrower calibration pattern and also contains substantial methodological debate about how large the effect is and how it should be measured.
